data.title: Hong Kong Legco to review tighter rules on access to land records amid concerns
data.description:
Hong Kong’s legislature will set up a subcommittee to examine proposed restrictions on access to land records following widespread public concern.
At the Legislative Council’s house committee meeting on Friday, lawmakers endorsed establishing the subcommittee to study proposed requirements and procedures under the Land Titles Regulation.
The move came after some legislators and the Hong Kong Journalists Association voiced objections on Wednesday after the government tabled eight pieces of subsidiary legislation – including the Land Titles Regulation covering land record search arrangements – at the Legco for negative vetting.
Under negative vetting, subsidiary legislation is first gazetted and then vetted by lawmakers later.
Most of the provisions, including the tightened search arrangements, are scheduled to take effect in the first half of next year.
On Friday, Legco legal adviser Timothy Tso recommended setting up a subcommittee on subsidiary legislation, noting that his team was still examining the details of the changes.
At least five legislators raised their hands in support, including Election Committee constituency members Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan, Andrew Lam Siu-lo and Thomas So Shiu-tsung, alongside Christine Fong Kwok-shan and Mark Chong Ho-fung.
“I also have concerns over whether referencing specific cases during legislative questioning could inadvertently breach the law [if my team has conducted land searches],” Roundtable lawmaker Chong told the South China Morning Post.
He added that when lawmakers conducted research or gathered real-life cases to address policy issues or assist enforcement – such as targeting public housing tenants who illegally own private property – there were fears of unwittingly crossing legal boundaries.
He noted that while the public previously relied on the media to investigate such matters, uncertainty remained over how individuals or lawmakers should proceed if they performed searches themselves.
He also said that no timeline has been set for when the subcommittee would meet, though the Legco secretariat was expected to issue a notice inviting interested lawmakers to join.

The new search arrangements represent the government’s latest step to tighten public access to information, following similar restrictions imposed on the vehicle and companies registries.
The government has maintained that the city currently does not restrict who can access land records and argued that the new arrangements aim to protect privacy while maintaining system transparency and efficiency.
Under the proposed regime, applicants must select from nine specified purposes to obtain essential property information, such as the names of current and former owners, purchase prices, registration dates, encumbrances, application forms and supporting documents for active entries.
These specific purposes include property valuation, due diligence for transactions, building management, legal proceedings, conducting academic and market research and conducting inspections in the public interest.
Applications filed on public interest grounds will be assessed individually by the registrar, who will consider whether the societal benefit outweighs privacy rights and whether the documents might be misused.
Meanwhile, access to historical records – such as past property transfers or complied building orders – will be restricted to 15 categories of applicants.
While the list does not explicitly include journalists, it permits applications from individuals declaring a public interest purpose, current or former property owners, and professionals.
Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan said she backed forming a subcommittee because many details remained unresolved, adding that the government needed to clarify the criteria and definition used to approve applications.
The Hong Kong Journalists Association previously criticised the proposals, stating that authorities had failed to justify the changes or consult the public, while warning that the restrictions would undermine society’s ability to monitor the property market.
Additional reporting by Ng Kang-chung

data.title: Sauce maker to close after 90 years, making way for Northern Metropolis
data.description:
One of Hong Kong’s last traditional sauce makers is to cease operations, ending its 90-year legacy, after authorities cleared land at its Kwu Tung factory on Friday.
Established in 1936, Kui Lee Sauce and Preserved Fruit confirmed to the South China Morning Post that it would close down once its remaining inventory at its shop in Wan Chai was sold.
“Our factory in Kwu Tung has halted production, and all remaining stock is at our retail shop. We will close permanently after selling through all inventory,” an employee of Kui Lee Sauce told an SCMP reporter, who posed as a customer.
As a time-honoured Hong Kong brand, Kui Lee has been passed down through three generations and is known for being “100 per cent made in Hong Kong”.
Having moved from Kowloon City to Kwu Tung in the 1960s, the factory has insisted on making soy sauce and vinegar using traditional sun-drying methods.
Its soy sauce has long been renowned in Hong Kong and has been exported to other markets in recent years, including Taiwan.
On Friday morning, more than 30 security guards and police officers were deployed to the Kui Lee sauce factory and Tong Kok Village in Kwu Tung to execute eviction notices.
The area is subject to a land resumption operation under the government’s Northern Metropolis megaproject, which aims to transform about 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into a technology hub and serve as an economic engine.
People wearing vests marked “NDA” – short for the New Development Areas under the Northern Metropolis strategy – were seen entering the sauce factory and spoke with the owner in a room for more than 30 minutes.

More than 12 security guards stood outside, while another dozen cordoned off the entrance and locked the steel gate.
Most of the guards left the factory at around 12.10pm after a notice was posted on the gate stating that the site had been taken over by the government. November 6 will be the final date for water and electricity supply and clearing items at the site.
Three security guards still stationed at the entrance were allowing workers temporary access to the factory through the gate.
The factory representatives declined to comment on the clearance.
The Lands Department’s clearance operation faced pushback from villagers on the site, many of whom had lived there for half a century.
A handful of residents were packing up the last of their belongings in homes they had lived in for decades, among them the Chan family.
“After all, we’ve lived here for more than 50 years. I feel reluctant to leave,” said Chan, a retiree in her seventies, standing in front of her house and wiping away tears with a towel. “This is half a century of memories.”
Her son, in his forties and born and raised in the house, was wrapping up a final batch of daily necessities with his wife.
“We were told the exact date of the land clearance not long ago, and our electricity was cut two days ago,” Chan’s daughter-in-law said.
“I was washing clothes when the power went off, and we could only use a flashlight to pack our things at night.”
She added that the water pipes had been destroyed by someone in recent days.
“We used to have a big family living here together for a whole life. Now we’re all separated,” she said.
Nearby, dozens of security guards and lands officials had surrounded another resident’s home and were preparing to lock it up, but a dispute broke out when the owner said they had not finished packing.
Staff prevented people from filming or getting closer to the site, citing “security concerns”.

data.title: Cambricon’s third quarter profit surges 148% amid push to replace Nvidia
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence chip giant Cambricon Technologies reported a 147.7 per cent surge in third-quarter profit on Friday, as the country’s aggressive push to replace Nvidia chips continues to fuel high growth among local chipmakers.
The Shanghai-listed chipmaker generated 1.4 billion yuan (US$210 million) in net profit for the three months ended September 30, up from 566.6 million yuan during the same period last year.
Revenue reached 3.5 billion yuan, an increase of 104.5 per cent from a year ago, according to its stock exchange filing. That was faster than the company’s 75.8 per cent revenue increase seen in the second quarter.
Cambricon attributed the revenue surge to its continuous market expansion and efforts to “facilitate the implementation of AI applications”. This top-line increase directly drove the year-on-year surge in total profit and net profit, the company said in the filing.
Shares of Cambricon closed up 5.5 per cent at 932.2 yuan ahead of the earnings release on Friday.
Earlier this week, Hygon Information Technology, another leading domestic AI chipmaker, posted third-quarter revenue of 5.9 billion yuan, an increase of 45.5 per cent year on year. Its net profit for the quarter surged 37.9 per cent year on year to 1 billion yuan.
The momentum at Cambricon and Hygon builds on Beijing’s initiative to develop a self-sufficient AI computing ecosystem, as the country accelerates the deployment of AI infrastructure powered by home-grown chips.

The two companies – regarded as top-tier players in the domestic AI chip sector – are moving rapidly to fill the market vacuum left by Washington’s export controls that have cut off China’s access to advanced AI accelerators from US chip giants like Nvidia.
Analysts said Cambricon’s earnings outlook depended largely on the commercialisation progress of its latest chips, which was in turn affected by supply chain pressures, especially the shortage of high bandwidth memory chips required for AI data centres.
“Cambricon delivered [its] MLU692 to a major cloud service provider in Q3 for testing, but we expect most revenue to be recognised in Q4,” Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a recent research report. “MLU580 shipments also remain limited as higher high bandwidth memory costs pressure unit economics.”
The MLU692 is part of Cambricon’s MLU690 chip series, also known as Siyuan 690. The series can outperform Nvidia’s H20 by 50 to 150 per cent when measured in “tokens per second”, a metric that essentially counts how many words or other data AI can process and spit out, according to an earlier Morgan Stanley report.
Hygon, meanwhile, faces high expectations for its next-generation central processing unit and its deep computing unit – a type of accelerator card designed specifically for AI.
The company said on Thursday that the progress was “on track” with key metrics such as compute density and interconnect bandwidth set to be upgraded, though mass production timelines remained pending.

data.title: China’s humanoid robots go job hunting in South Korea
data.description:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.
Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.
A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.
“China’s new generation of robot companies has global DNA and naturally looks overseas, and South Korea is one of the most important markets in the Asia-Pacific region,” said Ethan Qi, an associate director covering robotics at Counterpoint Research. The lack of locally built humanoid robots available at scale had created an opening for Chinese suppliers, he added.
Commercial foothold
Representatives of Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue in Seoul, agreed to buy UBTech’s lifelike U1 model after seeing its debut in Shenzhen in June, according to Sean Qin, overseas head of the company’s commercial robots division.
The robot, designed with a female appearance and standing 1.68 metres tall, cost around 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) and was delivered to the park last month, Qin said. UBTech entered the South Korean market as early as 2019 and had since sold more than 10,000 robots to dozens of corporate and government customers, he added.
In July, UBTech, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, also announced plans to trial humanoid robots on a South Korean automotive parts production line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker Ajin Industrial. Several UBTech models were undergoing on-site operational tests in the country, Qin said, without providing details.
“As a manufacturing powerhouse, South Korea already makes extensive use of robotic arms, autonomous mobile robots and other conventional systems,” he said. “The next step is to help workers become more productive in tasks that demand greater flexibility. That makes Korea a key market for UBTech and for humanoids more broadly.”
Zhang Yufeng, founder and CEO of Anyverse Dynamics, who previously worked with SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, said South Korea was “one of our most important overseas markets”.
The Beijing-based start-up teamed up with South Korean coffee chain Hollys at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August to test robots that serve drinks, clear tables and reset seats. The robots were currently undergoing trial operations at a cafe in Beijing, Zhang said.

South Korea ranked as China’s third-largest export market by value for “intelligent bionic robots” in the first nine months of 2026, behind the United States and Japan, according to Chinese customs data. Exports to South Korea totalled US$19.99 million, or 9.7 per cent of the US$206.95 million China shipped globally. China exported 16,559 robots to 108 countries and regions under the customs category, introduced this year, which covers humanoids and robot dogs.
Eight of China’s 10 top-selling humanoid robot makers had been testing the waters in South Korea through product certification, trademark filings and sales channels, according to a report by industry research platform Labsdeep that was cited by Electronic Times this month.
“We plan to begin trials in Korean cafes and other commercial service settings in the fourth quarter, before expanding into manufacturing,” Zhang said, noting that the company had been working on product certification for the market.
Seoul’s stringent Korea Certification requirements prompted UBTech to adapt its communications modules and radio frequency settings for local use, Qin said.
Factories as main testing ground
China’s robotics boom has spawned a wave of unicorn firms over the past two years, some of which have already begun shipping products at scale, backed by an extensive supply chain at home. Their push to find commercial applications to justify the investment and hype surrounding humanoid robots coincides with South Korea’s drive to deploy physical AI across its industrial base.
Seoul is prioritising the technology to strengthen manufacturing as its working-age population shrinks and potential economic growth slows. The government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (US$2.3 billion) in physical AI funding for 2027, more than triple this year’s level.
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources’ Manufacturing AI Transformation programme, dubbed M.AX, supports AI adoption and factory trials involving robots, including humanoids, with a target of 500 AI factories by 2030. The ministry has budgeted 1.1 trillion won for AI transformation this year.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said in August that the government would support factories operated by AI and robots, helping South Korea become “a global leader in manufacturing AI transformation by 2030”.
South Korea’s industrial heavyweights are also moving quickly.
LG Electronics is building its Data Factory in Seoul to train robots for industrial and household applications, while testing robots on its own production lines. Samsung Electronics established its Robotics eXperience division in July, targeting manufacturing before expanding into homes and retail. A bipedal robot designed to operate round the clock in manufacturing and logistics could debut at the CES annual consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas in January 2027, JoongAng Ilbo reported on Tuesday.
Hyundai Motor Group has begun training Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoids at its factory campus in the US state of Georgia, ahead of a planned 2028 deployment in manufacturing. Doosan Robotics has unveiled AI-powered sanding and palletising systems and is developing robot-control software, with support from Nvidia.
South Korea’s start-up ecosystem is also drawing fresh capital. AI and robotics accounted for 45 per cent of third-quarter investments tracked by The VC, a local start-up and venture capital investment database platform. Within physical AI, funding is flowing to robot makers as well as start-ups developing foundational models for robots and supplying training data.
The country offered a broad range of potential deployment sites in carmaking, shipbuilding and semiconductor manufacturing, Counterpoint’s Qi said. But gaining access was difficult for Chinese suppliers because they needed local customers willing to participate in proof-of-concept trials.
Partners and rivals
The growing presence of Chinese firms has stirred political debate. At a parliamentary audit on October 6, lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea brought robots from China’s Unitree and AgiBot to challenge the government over South Korea’s competitiveness in physical AI.
Lawmaker Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party questioned whether the robots had undergone security checks and accused the National Assembly of providing a stage for Chinese technology.
Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who is also the Science and Information and Communications Technology minister, urged South Korea to ramp up physical AI investment and development, pointing to China’s growing deployment of humanoids.
“China is also deploying more humanoid robots in the field and collecting data,” he said during a Physical AI Tech Week round table in Seoul on October 13, according to news outlet MoneyToday.
Bae questioned whether Korea’s plans were bold enough and called for higher targets to avoid regretting insufficient investment in the future. Companies also needed to shoulder greater responsibility because the government could not support every initiative, he said.
Park Young-hoon, head of the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency’s Shenzhen office, said he also saw room for cooperation.
“Companies need to explore new business opportunities using Shenzhen’s local supply chains and innovation capabilities while competing with Chinese technology companies,” he told local media outlet Newspim in October.
Anyverse Dynamics’ Zhang said he saw the two countries’ industrial strengths as “highly complementary”. South Korea combined global leadership in advanced manufacturing with a capacity for AI innovation, while China offered a comprehensive supply chain, a deep pool of engineering and AI talent, and rapid product iteration, he said.
For UBTech’s Qin, policies favouring domestic companies have not deterred Korean customers from considering Chinese suppliers. “The Korean customers we have dealt with are open to working with Chinese robot makers,” he said.

data.title: Former HSBC insurance veteran joins AIA in latest senior talent move
data.description:
Former HSBC Holdings global insurance head Edward Moncreiffe will join rival AIA Group as regional CEO from November 2, following a path taken by former HSBC Group chairman Mark Tucker, who returned to the Asia-Pacific region’s largest insurer as non-executive chairman last year.
Moncreiffe will oversee AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand, while serving on the group’s executive committee, according to a company statement issued on Friday. He will report to group CEO and president Lee Yuan Siong.
After 20 years at HSBC, Moncreiffe resigned as global insurance CEO in August. During his tenure, the lender’s insurance business became Hong Kong’s market leader in new life insurance premiums for four consecutive years and sold a record-breaking US$250 million life insurance policy in February 2024.
He is the second high-profile executive to move from HSBC to AIA. Tucker became AIA’s non-executive chairman in October last year after serving as the insurer’s group CEO and president between 2010 and 2017.
The appointment highlights intensifying competition for senior talent in the insurance and wealth management sector in Hong Kong and Asia, as growing numbers of wealthy customers use insurance products for wealth preservation and succession planning.
“I am delighted to be joining AIA, a company distinguished by its exceptional franchise, clear purpose and long-term commitment to Asia,” Moncreiffe said.
“AIA’s businesses in India, Sri Lanka, Australia and New Zealand each have distinct strengths, priorities and opportunities,” he said, adding that he would work with his new team to deliver long-term value for customers, partners and shareholders.
Moncreiffe holds a bachelor’s degree from Durham University and a master of business administration from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business. He is also a chartered insurer.
Lee said Moncreiffe’s “extensive international experience and strong track record of growing businesses and strengthening market positions” would help accelerate AIA’s next phase of growth.

data.title: Hong Kong marks hottest ‘Frost’ solar term on record at 32.1 degrees Celsius
data.description:
Hong Kong recorded its highest-ever temperature for the traditional Chinese calendar’s “Frost” solar term on Friday, with the weather forecaster warning of a very dry weekend ahead.
The Hong Kong Observatory said the temperature reached 32.1 degrees Celsius by 2.30pm.
Frost, the 18th of the Chinese lunisolar calendar’s 24 solar terms, began on October 23. The terms mark natural phenomena and seasonal changes.
Temperatures in the city have topped 30 degrees over the past few weeks, partly because of the effects of a super typhoon, El Nino and global warming.

The forecaster warned the public to prepare for a “fine and very dry” weekend, with a considerable difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures.
Humidity fell to 39 per cent on Friday and was forecast to drop further to 35 per cent on Saturday.
Earth science expert Professor Amos Tai Pui-kuen earlier explained that a “super” El Nino would make the city hotter, bringing more heat and increased evaporation.
Tai expected temperatures to fall gradually as winter approached but said the city would remain warm because of the lingering effects of the “super” El Nino.

data.title: Hong Kong constable paralysed in 2005 knife attack laid to rest with full honours
data.description:
Hong Kong’s top government officials and police officers have paid their final respects to a former constable who died 21 years after being left paralysed in an attack while on duty, during a funeral with full police honours.
Jacky Chu Chun-kwok, who died last month aged 52, was laid to rest on Friday following a service at the Universal Funeral Parlour in Hung Hom at 10.30am, which was attended by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung.
The mood was sombre as family members, friends, colleagues and senior officials bid farewell to Chu, formerly a constable with the Police Tactical Unit.
Holding Chu’s portrait, his wife, Chu Choi Yin-ping, wept alongside their daughter, Michelle, as they stepped out of the funeral parlour.
Outside, uniformed officers formed a contingent to salute the late constable, while members of the public lined the streets to mourn him.

Other senior government officials paying homage included Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming, Secretary for the Civil Service Ingrid Yeung Ho Poi-yan, as well as former police commissioner Dick Lee Ming-kwai. Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king and Executive Council convenor Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee were also present.
After the service, dozens of officers provided an honour guard escort as the cortege travelled to Cheung Sha Wan Police Station for a farewell ceremony at about 11am.
Chu’s coffin, draped with the Hong Kong flag, was carried by fellow officers and placed in a black police van converted into a hearse. At the police station, several officers bowed three times before the hearse.
Shortly after noon, the hearse left for Gallant Garden at Wo Hop Shek Cemetery, where Chu was laid to rest. The dedicated memorial and burial ground within the cemetery is reserved for civil servants who have died in the line of duty.

Chu died last month after spending 21 years paralysed and bedridden. On the morning of July 19, 2005, he was critically injured while on solo patrol when a man stabbed him in the neck with a six-inch knife.
The attacker, Liu Chi-yung, had been carrying the knife with the intention of robbing pedestrians when Chu stopped him for an identity check outside the Po On Road Municipal Services Building in Cheung Sha Wan.
When the then 30-year-old constable grew suspicious and confronted him, Liu pulled out the knife, stabbed Chu in the neck and fled.
Chu pursued the attacker but eventually collapsed from excessive blood loss. Oxygen deprivation to the brain left him completely paralysed and in a vegetative state.
He was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) in 2006.

data.title: Chinese stocks bounce back from bear market on suspected state support
data.description:
Chinese stocks rebounded on Friday after a sell-off dragged the benchmark index into a bear market, as surging trading volumes in the nation’s biggest exchange-traded funds (ETFs) pointed to possible state buying and major companies at the centre of the artificial intelligence trade sought to reassure investors.
The CSI 300 Index rose 1 per cent to 4,075.44 as of 2.06pm local time, reversing an earlier decline of as much as 2 per cent. Turnover in several key ETFs tracking the gauge surged, suggesting that Central Huijin Investment and other state-backed funds might have intervened to stem further losses.
The benchmark technically entered bear-market territory a day earlier after sliding 20 per cent from its June peak.
Technology stocks led the rebound. The ChiNext 50 index rallied 2.9 per cent after the nation’s top three makers of optical transceivers used in AI data centres either unveiled share buy-back plans or reassured investors that operations remained normal.
The Star Market 50 index, which tracks some of the nation’s biggest chipmakers, including Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp and Cambricon Technologies, gained 1.4 per cent.
The dramatic turn indicated that government intervention still wielded substantial influence on China’s stock market, which Beijing views as a key funding source for its tech self-reliance strategy.
China Securities Regulatory Commission chairman Wu Qing pledged this week to attract more long-term capital by further opening up the onshore market to foreign investors and broadening the range of ETF products.
Stocks had come under pressure earlier this week as concerns mounted over China’s growth outlook after Beijing refrained from introducing fresh stimulus measures and the crowded global AI trade continued to unravel.
Investors also remained wary of the fallout from new taxes on offshore trusts held by wealthy Chinese families.
The recent market weakness could be linked to selling by major shareholders seeking to raise funds for tax payments ahead of the 90-day grace period that expired on Thursday, according to Hua An Securities.
Global investment banks from UBS Group to Nomura Holdings said this week that China would stick to the current policy approach through the rest of the year after third-quarter data indicated that the nation was on track to meet its annual growth target of between 4.5 and 5 per cent.
“Stronger exports and faster fiscal execution have reduced the urgency for further policy easing, with subdued domestic demand and household deleveraging continuing to constrain a broader earnings,” said Laura Wang, a strategist at Morgan Stanley, in a note on Thursday.
“Meanwhile, elevated US Treasury yields and renewed expectations of US Federal Reserve tightening remain headwinds for global liquidity and offshore equity valuations.”

data.title: Market sell-off, tax scrutiny and growth: key figures shaping investor sentiment
data.description:
As regional equities tumbled and hopes for investor stimulus faded, the Hang Seng Index fell to a seven-month low. Attention also remained focused on Beijing’s intensified scrutiny of offshore wealth and tax compliance. Macroeconomic data pointed to steady, if uneven, domestic momentum.
Here are the core figures capturing market attention this week.
Hong Kong stocks suffer steepest drop in 7 months
The Hang Seng Index sank 3.03 per cent in a single session to 22,934.68 points, its worst performance since March, as slowing profit growth among major tech firms and reduced expectations for stimulus weighed on sentiment.
Investors were also concerned about potential share sales ahead of Beijing’s Thursday deadline for offshore trust gains. Shares of Chinese toymaker Bloks Group plunged after its chairman sold a 1.6 per cent stake for HK$250 million (US$31.9 million), a move that some market watchers linked to liquidity needs arising from the new tax regime.
China’s tax workforce recruitment drive accelerates
China’s 2027 national civil service recruitment plan includes 24,013 tax-related positions, accounting for more than 67 per cent of all vacancies, up from over 65 per cent a year earlier.
The expansion of the tax workforce is drawing attention from businesses and wealthy families as compliance climbs higher on the policy agenda and authorities intensify enforcement efforts.
Treasury yields slip below 5 per cent threshold
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note dropped below 5 per cent on Thursday for the first time in a month. The benchmark fell as low as 4.95 per cent in intraday trading, while yields on 30-year and five-year bonds also declined.
China’s economy grows 4.6 per cent
China’s economy expanded 4.6 per cent year on year in the first three quarters, meeting the lower end of official full-year targets while highlighting a persistent divide between strong exports and weak domestic demand.
Hong Kong secures strategic investment pledges
Hong Kong on Thursday attracted its seventh batch of 18 strategic enterprises, including Solana and Johnson & Johnson, which pledged more than HK$10 billion in investment and 1,600 high-end jobs to bolster the city’s tech and financial sectors.
US banks pile into dim sum bonds
According to a Bank of America report, US lenders helped drive a 68 per cent surge in issuance of offshore yuan-denominated bonds – known as dim sum bonds – lifting total fundraising to 774 billion yuan (US$116 billion). The surge comes as Wall Street increasingly taps Chinese capital markets even as the yield premium over dollar funding continues to narrow.

data.title: Super Typhoon Champi disrupts more than 70 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan
data.description:
More than 70 flights between Hong Kong and Taiwan have been cancelled as Super Typhoon Champi approaches the island ahead of a possible landfall later on Friday.
As of noon on Friday, more than 30 flights between the city and Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport had been cancelled, according to a South China Morning Post check of the Hong Kong airport’s website.
Nine outbound flights to Kaohsiung International Airport and Taichung International Airport were also cancelled.
The affected flights included services operated by Cathay Pacific Airways, HK Express, Hong Kong Airlines, Starlux Airlines, China Airlines and EVA Air.
More than 30 inbound flights from Taiwan were also cancelled as Champi’s rainbands swept across the island. Torrential downpours and fierce gusts have been forecast.

Despite the storm, a Greater Bay Airlines flight to Taipei and an HK Express flight to Kaohsiung took off on Friday morning.
Cathay Pacific, its budget arm HK Express and Hong Kong Airlines said they would waive ticket change fees for affected passengers.
At noon, Champi – whose name means frangipani in Khmer – was centred about 290km (180 miles) southeast of Taipei. The storm has already caused one death.
The Hong Kong Observatory has forecast it to move north-northwest at about 15 km/h over the seas east of Taiwan.
Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said the storm’s 320km radius would cover most of the island on Friday. Its peak impact was expected to last through the night before it moved away towards southern Japan late on Saturday.

data.title: How Hong Kong’s yuan bond market became a key funding source for global banks
data.description:
Hong Kong’s offshore yuan bond market is becoming an increasingly important funding source for global banks, with US lenders driving a surge in issuance even as the currency’s traditional funding advantage over the dollar narrows.
The shift offers a glimpse of how financial ties between Wall Street and China are evolving despite geopolitical tensions. For US banks, the attraction increasingly lies in access to Chinese capital rather than lower borrowing costs.
Offshore yuan-denominated bonds, known as dim sum bonds, reached 774 billion yuan (US$116 billion) in issuance as of October 20, up 68 per cent from a year earlier, according to a Bank of America (BofA) Global Research report on Wednesday. Financial institutions accounted for 57 per cent of total supply, with issuance from the sector rising 139 per cent year on year.
Foreign financial institutions issued 333 billion yuan of bonds, up 169 per cent from a year earlier and more than double their average annual issuance between 2022 and 2025. US banks led the surge, raising 167 billion yuan, an increase of 130 billion yuan from a year earlier.
US global systemically important banks have raised the equivalent of US$22 billion through offshore yuan bonds this year, making the yuan their third-largest funding currency after the US dollar and euro, overtaking the sterling, BofA said.
The surge has continued despite a fading cost advantage. At the end of September, yields on three-year yuan government bonds, after currency hedging, were only about 0.1 percentage points below comparable US Treasury yields, the bank said. The rise of offshore Chinese capital had “fundamentally changed the rationale” for yuan issuance, it added.
The question is no longer whether the offshore yuan market will continue to grow, but rather how quickly regulators will allow offshore yuan capital pools to expand
BofA Global Research
The market was also expanding as China’s offshore US dollar bond market shrunk, having contracted to about US$400 billion from its 2021 peak, amid a collapse in property-sector issuance and corporate deleveraging, according to the report.
The outstanding dim sum bond market reached 1.9 trillion yuan, or about US$284 billion, nearly quadrupling from the end of 2021 and growing to about 70 per cent of the size of the offshore dollar market, the bank said.
Demand from mainland Chinese investors is supporting the expansion.
Holdings through the southbound Bond Connect scheme – which allows mainland investors to access Hong Kong’s offshore bond market – reached 1 trillion yuan at the end of August, up 85 per cent year on year, after authorities broadened participation by institutional investors, BofA said. Nearly 30 per cent of dim sum bonds issued this year had an average life exceeding seven years.
Chinese technology companies are also tapping the market to finance investment in artificial intelligence. Their offshore yuan issuance rose to 57 billion yuan this year, broadly matching their US dollar bond issuance.
BofA estimated that China would need to invest US$1.5 trillion in AI-related capital expenditure between 2026 and 2030, including about US$900 billion by major internet platforms.
More than 75 per cent of technology-sector yuan bonds issued this year had maturities of more than seven years, the report said.
Future growth will depend partly on Beijing’s willingness to expand channels for mainland money to flow offshore. Authorities have raised the annual southbound Bond Connect quota to 800 billion yuan from 500 billion yuan after the previous limit was nearly exhausted.
The new quota was equivalent to more than 40 per cent of the existing dim sum bond market, BofA said, making policy decisions a key determinant on future growth.
“The question is no longer whether the [offshore yuan] market will continue to grow, but rather how quickly regulators will allow offshore yuan capital pools to expand,” the report added.

data.title: 2 women arrested over alleged child abuse after girl, 11, posts plea for help
data.description:
Two women have been arrested in Hong Kong on suspicion of child abuse after an 11-year-old girl posted videos on social media in a plea for help, capturing moments of emotional distress inside her home.
Police arrested a 61-year-old local woman and a 43-year-old foreign woman in Wong Tai Sin on Friday on suspicion of ill-treatment or neglect by those in charge of a child or young person.
The girl, found with red and swollen limbs, was sent to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Yau Ma Tei in a conscious state on Thursday and later transferred to the Hong Kong Children’s Hospital in Kowloon Bay, according to police.
The arrest followed the circulation of two distressing video clips recorded secretly by the child inside a home setting.
In the first video clip, filmed covertly, a man was heard aggressively shouting and insulting the sobbing child in a flat, hurling profanity and abusive phrases such as “even a kindergarten kid is smarter than you” and “you are just like your terrible mother”.
In the second video clip, the terrified girl is seen seeking refuge inside a room, pleading for help to the camera: “I need some help, my family is going crazy.”

Before she could finish her sentence, a woman began aggressively pounding on the door, screaming at her to shut up, leaving the girl trembling and weeping in fear.
Police said they received a referral of a suspected ill-treatment of a child by family members.
The offence carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment under Section 27 of the Offences Against the Person Ordinance (Cap. 212).
The suspects are in police custody as the investigation continues.
The South China Morning Post has reached out to the girl’s school, the Education Bureau and the Social Welfare Department for comment.

data.title: DeepSeek, MiniMax secure open-source licences days after new China export rules
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence model developers DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed export registration procedures and proceeded with open-source releases and overseas licensing activities, according to Chinese state media, days after Beijing moved to tighten oversight on AI tech transfers.
Yuyuan Tantian, an influential social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, reported on Thursday evening that the two AI companies had completed the required registrations after Beijing proposed adding export control restrictions and prohibitions to 23 AI-related technologies last week, covering large language models, AI agents and computing clusters.
The draft proposal released by the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology, which also included provisions that came into immediate effect requiring official registration for the covered technologies, raised questions about whether Beijing was restricting Chinese AI companies from expanding overseas, particularly as the country’s open-weight models have gained international adoption.
However, the Yuyuan Tantian post said the proposed measures were intended to establish clearer regulatory boundaries rather than shut the door on Chinese AI technology exports.
“Simply put, AI companies can continue with their commercialisation efforts as usual. Once the relevant measures are officially implemented, the vast majority of artificial intelligence technologies will still be freely exportable,” Yuyuan Tantian said.
The CCTV-affiliated post acknowledged the overseas speculation over whether Beijing was shifting its stance on open-source AI, which it has championed as a superior alternative to the closed-source approach of the US AI industry.

However, it highlighted the approvals for DeepSeek and MiniMax as indicative of China’s continued stance of “encouraging openness,” urging businesses to “remain calm in the face of the new regulations”.
Both companies have open-sourced major updates in recent days, with Hangzhou-based DeepSeek upgrading its V4.1 Flash model and open-sourcing its in-house inference framework, while Shanghai-based MiniMax open-sourced its M3.1 model on Friday.
The registration requirements covered transfers of technology ownership, overseas licensing arrangements and changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities. Companies are required to register relevant transactions with MOFCOM before proceeding.
According to Yuyuan Tantian, authorities began preparing the proposed rules in the first half of the year, consulting research institutions, industry associations and leading companies before publishing the draft document.
It noted that Beijing was seeking to distinguish between the transfer of underlying AI technology abroad – which it would clamp down on for national security reasons – and providing commercial AI services overseas, which it would continue to encourage.
The assessment echoes remarks from a MOFCOM spokesperson last week, who said that overseas access to Chinese AI models through application programming interfaces, official websites and mobile applications would not be covered by the proposed export controls.
For the open-sourcing of AI technologies, the spokesperson said that expedited “automatic licensing” measures would be applied, as quickly as “immediate reporting and export”.
Beijing’s bolstering of its tech export control regime comes as the US mulls further restrictions on Chinese access to cutting-edge US technologies, including major congressional bills that would further clamp down on exports of advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment.
The US Department of Homeland Security on Tuesday also ordered all US federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek and third-party tools built on it, a move that Beijing criticised as being discriminatory.
In its post, Yuyuan Tantian drew a line between the US and Chinese approach to export controls, claiming that China “is not taking the path” set by the US of using such measures to isolate competitors and maintain its global technological leadership.
“Our revision is a routine process carried out in accordance with laws and regulations,” it said, while noting that it would also help China gain greater influence in global technological competition.

data.title: As Asia offices hand over tasks to AI agents, market forecast to grow 14-fold
data.description:
The artificial intelligence agent software market across Asia, Australia and New Zealand is set to expand more than 14-fold by 2030, according to research firm Omdia, as Chinese tech companies increasingly deploy automated tools across office and industrial operations.
During its annual event in Beijing on Thursday, Omdia forecast that regional market revenue, which included mainland China and Hong Kong, would reach US$11.2 billion in 2030, up from an estimated US$782 million this year. Over the same period, the agentic share of the region’s AI software revenue was projected to rise to 12.3 per cent from 1.7 per cent.
AI agents use models to autonomously plan and carry out multi-step tasks – such as data analysis, report writing and software operations – allowing users to delegate work that would otherwise require repeated instructions.
China’s State Council has set targets for the penetration of next-generation intelligent devices and agents to exceed 70 per cent by 2027 and 90 per cent by 2030 under its “AI Plus” initiative.
Major Chinese tech companies are accelerating deployment to capture growing adoption in their own market.
Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, unveiled AgentCore last month. The enterprise platform is designed to help businesses build, run and manage AI agents, including monitoring their performance and connecting them to existing business systems.
Tencent Holdings is also expanding its WorkBuddy agent workspace, which the company said can edit Word documents, Excel spreadsheets and PowerPoint presentations directly, and connect to services including Notion and GitHub to retrieve information and carry out tasks.

In an August report, Moody’s Ratings expected the combined capital spending of Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance, to more than double to about US$140 billion this year from US$65 billion in 2025.
Cloud services remain the main channel for monetising AI, Moody’s said, with lower-cost open-source models accelerating enterprise adoption in China. However, intense price competition and the smaller scale of Chinese cloud businesses left them less able than their US peers to fund further AI infrastructure expansion from cloud cash flow, it said.
Maximising return on investment remains a priority for enterprises adopting AI. “Using more tokens does not mean producing more value,” Omdia chief analyst Su Lian Jye said, referring to the units of data processed by AI models and a common basis for charging customers.
Su said businesses needed to assess the value of AI’s output and improve efficiency by matching tasks with appropriate models. Chinese companies were also using open-source models to attract developers and users, although deploying them still required substantial engineering expertise, he said.
The push into AI agents is also opening a new front in competition among cloud providers.
Integrating models, software and computing infrastructure could make customers harder to win away, as moving an agent-based application to another cloud could require transferring both the model and the optimisations behind it, making migration more complicated, Su said.

data.title: Hong Kong security chief vows accountability, reforms ahead of Tai Po fire report
data.description:
The Fire Services Department will bear “ultimate responsibility” for following up on fire safety complaints across Hong Kong, the security chief has said, pledging legal reforms after the deadly Tai Po blaze, as an independent committee’s report is expected to identify the department as among those responsible.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung made the pledge a day after the judge-led committee submitted its final report to the government. Sources said the report would identify failings by the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit that contributed to the blaze.
During earlier public evidential hearings, counsel for the committee criticised the Fire Services Department for failing to detect that the housing estate’s fire alarm system had been deactivated and for avoiding its statutory duties.
Speaking on a radio programme on Friday, Tang said the government had taken steps to address the shortcomings and would hold those responsible fully accountable.
“Over the past year, we have implemented many administrative measures on [handling] large-scale fires and fire alarm device malfunctions. A series of legal reforms will be rolled out too,” he said.
“The Fire Services Department has admitted its ‘ultimate responsibility’, which means when anyone files a complaint about fire [safety] to the department, even if it’s not directly under our purview, we would follow up until another department takes over.”

Following the blaze, the department stepped up inspections of fire services installations and put forward legislative proposals to strengthen their regulation.
Asked whether he or his colleagues were mentally prepared to be held accountable for the fire, Tang cited Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s pledge that “anyone found to be responsible will be held accountable”.
The fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on November 26, 2025, killed 168 people and displaced almost 5,000.
The South China Morning Post earlier learned that a redacted version of the report could be made public as early as next week.
Separately, Tang said Hong Kong would remain vigilant ahead of the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in mid-November, as visits by political leaders would inevitably pose security risks to the city.
He said authorities would prepare for potential attempts to enter the mainland via Hong Kong to carry out dangerous and illegal activities, as well as drone flights from the city aimed at disrupting the summit.
They would also prepare for possible visits to Hong Kong by leaders or dignitaries, although he expected any impact on the public to be limited.
Drawing comparisons with social unrest in France, Tang said Hong Kong was capable of managing similar situations, but he urged the public to remain vigilant even in peaceful times and think critically to avoid being incited, given potential national security risks.

data.title: Wine walks, star chefs and fresh flavours: enjoying the Wine and Dine Festival
data.description:
The annual Hong Kong Wine and Dine Festival later this month promises more booths and longer hours to help attract over 168,000 visitors.
The South China Morning Post unpacks what is on offer so you can enjoy the event to the fullest.
1. What is the festival and when is it open?
Organised by the Tourism Board under the theme “Taste the World’s Best,” the festival will be held from October 29 to November 1 at the Central Harbourfront, opening at 7.30pm on the first day and 1pm on the following three days.
For the first time, on October 30 and 31, the event will extend its opening hours until 1am.
2. What’s new at the Wine and Dine Festival this year?
The four-day festival will be larger than last year’s, with more than 340 booths, an increase of over 10 per cent. The festival footprint will also be extended to Tamar Park.
The event will feature guided wine walks for the first time, where participants can experience more than 20 masterclasses led by experts who will guide them through wine tastings and share professional insights.
The Tourism Board will subsequently launch “Hong Kong Gourmet Month” in November, featuring limited-edition dishes and dining discounts throughout the month. Visitors to the Wine and Dine Festival can present their ticket stubs to enjoy exclusive offers at selected restaurants, retailers and business associations.

3. What are the culinary highlights and special tasting events?
Highlights include the Grand Wine Pavilion, a designated area for premium wine, the Tasting Room restaurant featuring five renowned chefs, and the Hotel Boulevard showcasing signature dishes from 26 hotels.
The Grand Wine Pavilion will bring together fine wines and delicacies from around 31 countries and regions, including Australia, Canada and South Korea.
It will also feature wine selections from top Bordeaux chateaux, including renowned bottles such as Mouton Rothschild Pauillac 1er Cru 1982, a prized wine from one of Bordeaux’s “first growth” estates and the legendary 1982 vintage.
At the Tasting Room restaurant, diners can enjoy dishes made by famous chefs including Edward Lee, the Korean-American who made his name in Netflix’s cooking survival show Culinary Class Wars, and Michelin-starred masters including Yoda Chen Zhiping and Thierry Marx who will create a collaborative banquet alongside three other chefs.
The event will also feature local “Only in Hong Kong” flavours, including innovative combinations such as black sesame soy milk pudding tart.
The Hotel Boulevard will gather chefs from 26 prestigious hotels at the Central Harbourfront, each serving up signature dishes, including Hong Kong-style satay beef bun from Kowloon Shangri-La and 3 Signature Pandan Cake with Coconut Ice Cream from The Fullerton Ocean Park Hotel Hong Kong.
4. What special benefits or exclusive offers are available?
Tickets for the festival are HK$40 (US$5.13) per person and HK$20 each for children aged three to 11. Each tasting token costs HK$25.
Locals and visitors can purchase a Grand Wine Pass or Tasting Pass via Trip.com at a special discounted price, with complimentary admission included. Grand Wine Pass packages start from just HK$558 (valued at HK$900) and allow visitors to enjoy a wide range of signature activities at the Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival.
American Express card members enjoy exclusive benefits, including a special presale price on the Premium Wine Pass and 20 per cent off when adding consumption tokens at the festival.

data.title: Hong Kong elderly urged to stay indoors as air pollution spikes to serious levels
data.description:
Severe haze in Hong Kong over the past two days has prompted a government warning of serious health risks, with experts urging the elderly and vulnerable to stay indoors until sunset.
Air quality health risk levels at some of Hong Kong’s roadside monitoring stations rose on Wednesday and Thursday, with experts attributing the surge to elevated ozone levels caused by sunlight and high temperatures and warning that conditions were likely to persist over the next few days.
On Wednesday afternoon, the Air Quality Health Index issued by the Environmental Protection Department reached a “serious” health risk level at its Tuen Mun station, where it remained for two hourly readings.
The pollution persisted on Thursday, with Central/Western, Southern, Tsuen Wan, Tuen Mun and Sha Tin stations recording “high” health risk levels at 4pm. An hour later, the Southern station reached a “very high” level.
The hourly readings eventually began to fall in the evening.

Ho Kin-fai, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Jockey Club School of Public Health and Primary Care, said light winds had brought pollutants to the city, which, combined with high temperatures and sunlight this week, intensified photochemical smog activity – the major factor leading to the formation of ozone.
“Ozone remains the primary reason for the high health risk readings in the past two days, although it has occurred in different locations,” Ho said. “The situation may likely persist over the next few days.”
He said elderly and vulnerable people should remain mindful of air quality when the index is at the “high” health risk level.
Launched in 2013, the index tells residents of the short-term health risks posed by air pollution. It analyses three-hour average concentrations of four major pollutants, namely ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, and fine particulate matter – PM2.5 and PM10 – on a scale from 1 to 10, as well as 10+.
When the health risk level is “high”, the department advises children, the elderly and people with existing heart or respiratory conditions to reduce outdoor physical activity, especially in areas with heavy traffic. They should stay indoors when the index reaches the “serious” level.
For healthy adults who want to exercise outdoors, Ho suggested shortening workout durations or running later at night, as ozone levels gradually declined after sunset.

Air quality was usually worse in winter compared with other seasons due to meteorological conditions, said Leung Wing-mo, a former assistant director at the Hong Kong Observatory.
During winter, the northeast monsoon could bring air pollutants from mainland China over to Hong Kong, Leung said, though he added that air quality in the Pearl River Delta region had improved over the past two decades.
Wind speed also played a role, he noted, as stronger winds created turbulence that lifted ground-level pollutants high into the atmosphere.
Cold spells influenced by the northeast monsoon also tend to last a few days at a time, meaning conditions may ease periodically, according to Leung.
Cooler temperatures were another factor, he said. As cool air near the surface settles in, the denser, cooler air beneath the warmer air leads to a higher probability of “temperature inversion”, slowing the dispersion of pollutants and causing them to accumulate near the ground.
Leung said it was challenging to determine whether Tropical Cyclone Champi had affected Hong Kong’s air quality, given the presence of other competing factors.
However, he noted that because Champi was a “big and intense typhoon”, its potential effect on Hong Kong through subsiding air could not be ruled out.
According to the city’s forecaster, Champi will move towards the seas east of Taiwan on Friday, before it is likely to steer northwards towards Japan and Korea.
Under the influence of its subsiding air, weather along the Guangdong coast would remain very hot through the latter half of the week, the forecaster added.

data.title: Unitree developing AI system to let humanoid robots improve themselves
data.description:
Unitree Robotics is developing a “self-evolving” feedback loop designed to allow humanoid robots to write code, run simulations and improve their real-world performance independently, founder Wang Xingxing said, in a move that mirrors a broader push towards “self-improving” artificial intelligence.
Speaking on Thursday at a physical AI conference hosted by Unitree in Hangzhou, Wang unveiled the project, dubbed “Unitree Rehearsal”, which he called the company’s most important initiative of the year.
The project sought to shift robotics development away from labour-intensive manual programming towards a continuous, autonomous feedback loop, he said. Under the system in development, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulations before running trials on physical robots.
While humans could still help assess performance and provide feedback, Wang said the ultimate goal was to create an automated cycle that could exponentially accelerate the development of robotics algorithms.
“In the past, every robotics engineer had to write code and debug manually, which is relatively inefficient,” Wang said. “As AI models improve, we expect them to take on more of the planning and iteration, reducing the need for human intervention.”
Leading AI companies had already begun using models to generate code and gather data under human guidance, Wang said, arguing that robotics firms could follow a similar blueprint. Unlike digital software, however, robots also had to navigate environmental unpredictability and mechanical errors, he said.
The comments came just days after Wang predicted that advances in OpenAI’s GPT-6 model could spur a broader robotics breakthrough within one to two years. His latest speech focused on the critical steps needed to translate AI model improvements into real-world utility.
In a video shown at the event, robots developed by Unitree used GPT-6 to map routes and plan movements without task-specific training, though the presentation did not demonstrate how consistently the machines could replicate that behaviour in unfamiliar environments.
While large AI models could handle robot planning and navigation, Wang said the biggest challenge was “aligning the AI model’s inputs and outputs with those of a real robot”.
If that challenge could be overcome, humanoid robots could be tidying rooms on command as early as 2027, Wang suggested, though he offered 2028 as a more realistic estimate.
Unitree’s upbeat road map echoed recent comments from Elon Musk. On Wednesday, the Tesla CEO told the US carmaker’s earnings call that humanoid robots could eventually become “the biggest product on Earth” and outnumber humans. He cautioned, however, that Tesla still faced about a year of development hurdles with its Optimus robot.
Data, however, points to a challenging transition from laboratory to living room. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index found that robots succeeded in only 12 per cent of real-world household tasks during evaluations, despite performing significantly better in simulation.

data.title: Fresh Hong Kong graduates feel AI impact as degree pay advantage narrows
data.description:
Fresh Hong Kong graduates are increasingly feeling the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) as they enter the workforce, human resources experts have said, after a survey found the starting salaries for degree holders and sub-degree graduates had narrowed.
The results of the latest annual survey by Baptist University found the disparity between the starting salaries of bachelor’s degree and sub-degree graduates narrowed by 17 per cent, or HK$500 (US$63.70), from HK$3,000 last year to HK$2,500 this year compared with 2025.
The experts urged the government to adjust its education strategies by taking into consideration the effects of AI on the job market while also encouraging students not to treat the technology as a threat.
“AI may be one reason behind the narrowing salary gap between degree levels, as some companies are unwilling to pay more for people with higher degrees when AI can help employees handle the same work,” Alexa Chow Yee-ping, managing director of human resources consultancy ACTS Consulting, said.
The survey covered more than 270,000 employees at 78 companies in Hong Kong, 38 in Macau and 105 in nine Guangdong province cities, which together form the Greater Bay Area.
It also found Hong Kong workers received smaller pay rises this year, at 2.3 per cent compared with 2.5 per cent in 2025, while the starting salaries of university graduates showed no clear upward trend.

“We expected the results from this period to look better as it covers most of this year’s pay adjustments in January, April and July,” Chow said. “And in the first half of last year, Hong Kong’s performance in GDP growth was relatively strong.”
Hong Kong raised its full-year growth forecast for 2026 to between 3.5 and 4.5 per cent from between 2.5 per cent and 3.5 per cent previously after better-than-expected performance in the first half of this year.
Chow explained that while the survey found the starting salaries for bachelor’s degree and sub-degree graduates had drawn closer, the situation varied by sector.
“In professional sectors such as healthcare and technology, where demand remains, the threshold will not easily be lowered,” she said.
Chow advised students to weigh their interests with practical considerations, in particular, whether the jobs they were considering were likely to be done by AI.
Labour sector lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, said the government should adjust its education policies in light of the shift.
“Hong Kong now has universities of applied sciences. I hope more can be scaled up to train young people for AI-related industries or emerging sectors, so that they can work in the emerging industries in the Northern Metropolis in the future and reduce human resources mismatch,” he said.
The Northern Metropolis project, announced in 2021, aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) of land into an engine for economic growth and a housing hub.
A separate survey by the non-government Hong Kong Institute of Human Resource Management, released in September, found that local employees received an average pay rise of 2.8 per cent this year.
After inflation, the real increase was 1.1 per cent, the lowest since the Covid-19 pandemic that roiled the city from 2020 to 2023.
Institute president Ian Choy Jing-man said fresh graduates were likely to feel the impact of slower pay growth most acutely.
“Fresh graduates mostly start at the general or supporting staff level, so their salary increments are likely to be on par with that group, which is growing more slowly than some of the other categories we surveyed,” he said.
Choy urged young people to treat AI as a tool rather than a threat. “Learn how to collaborate with it. It’s not your competition. And it’s definitely not stopping you from getting into the job market,” he said.
“But if you are equipped with the necessary AI skills, then you will come out on top of the competition.”
